questions.q: What does "data classification" fundamentally require, beyond just picking a labeling tool?
options: A named data owner accountable for deciding a dataset's sensitivity tier, and a consistent mechanism for that label to travel with the data
A single global sensitivity tier applied identically to every dataset in the organization
Nothing beyond installing a DLP product — classification is a built-in feature of any DLP tool
An agreement with the cloud provider to classify the data on the customer's behalf
questions.explain: Classification is an organizational exercise before a technical one: a data owner has to decide the tier, and a consistent labeling mechanism has to carry that decision with the data wherever it goes — otherwise the classification drifts out of date or gets lost.

questions.q: How does a Microsoft Purview sensitivity label differ from an AWS Macie finding?
options: They are functionally identical in every respect

A Purview label is embedded in the file and persists as it moves; a Macie finding is a discovery-based, continuously refreshed inventory of sensitive content found inside objects that were never manually labeled
Macie embeds a persistent label in every S3 object automatically; Purview only produces a one-time report
Neither one has anything to do with sensitive content detection
questions.explain: Purview labels are embedded in the file itself and survive downloads, email, and storage moves. Macie takes the opposite approach — since most S3 data was never manually labeled, it scans and discovers sensitive content, surfacing findings rather than attaching a persistent label.

questions.q: What happens to a DLP policy when it's deployed without any prior data classification?
options: It performs exactly as well as a classification-informed policy, since DLP tools classify internally
It automatically pulls classification data from the cloud provider's billing system
It refuses to run at all until classification is configured
It is forced to infer sensitivity from content inspection alone — regex, keywords, pattern matching — producing predictable false positives and false negatives
questions.explain: Without classification answering "how sensitive is this," a DLP engine has to guess from content alone, which produces false positives (e.g., blocking a training document with a sample card number) and false negatives (sensitive content with no detectable pattern sailing through).

questions.q: Which scenario is a classic false negative for a pattern-matching-only DLP rule?
options: A confidential business strategy document with no credit card numbers or SSNs, just sensitive context, passes through undetected because there's no pattern for it to match
A document with a real customer Social Security number gets correctly blocked
A training document with a sample credit card number gets blocked by mistake
A public marketing document gets blocked by mistake
questions.explain: A false negative is sensitive content that goes undetected. A strategy document with no regex-matchable pattern (no SSNs, no card numbers) has nothing for pattern-matching to catch, even though its business sensitivity is real.

questions.q: What is the practical order of operations this lesson recommends for protecting sensitive data?
options: Buy and configure a DLP tool first, then worry about classification later if false positives become a problem
Apply encryption to everything, then skip classification and DLP entirely
Identify data owners and define sensitivity tiers, apply labels (manually or via discovery), and only then write DLP policies keyed to those labels
Classification and DLP should be configured completely independently, since they solve unrelated problems
questions.explain: The sequence is: identify owners, define the needed tiers, apply labels (Purview auto-labeling or Macie discovery), and only then write DLP policies keyed to those labels. Reversing that order leaves a team tuning pattern-matching rules indefinitely.
